patient.history_present_illness: Mr. V. is a 70-year-old Hispanic man with compensated alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD 7), a known large spontaneous splenorenal portosystemic shunt (found incidentally 18 months ago and not treated), hypertension, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes. He is brought to the ED by his wife with an 8-hour history of confusion, disorientation, and slow speech — the fourth such episode over 18 months. The first three episodes were evaluated by neurology as outpatient and inpatient; MRI brain showed no acute DWI lesion on two occasions; a cardiology workup including echocardiogram and 30-day event monitor was unrevealing; a TIA diagnosis was maintained on the basis of age, vascular risk factors (hypertension, ex-smoker, diabetes), and episodic presentation. He was started on aspirin 81 mg after the second episode. Additionally, outpatient neurology labelled episodes of morning confusion as 'sundowning from MCI.' He has no prior overt HE episodes documented, no ascites, no history of GI bleeding. His outpatient hepatology notes from 6 months ago documented: 'liver synthetic function preserved; AST/ALT mildly elevated; bilirubin and INR normal; MELD 7; no intervention required for the known splenorenal shunt at this time.' On arrival, his wife notes the episode began after a large protein-rich meal (steak dinner). He has not had a bowel movement in 2 days.

output.query: hepatic encephalopathy spontaneous portosystemic shunt compensated cirrhosis hyperammonemia

results.title: AASLD/EASL 2014 Practice Guideline: Hepatic Encephalopathy in Chronic Liver Disease
results.summary: HE occurs in the setting of portosystemic shunting (including large spontaneous shunts) and does not require overt hepatic synthetic failure. Large spontaneous portosystemic shunts (e.g., splenorenal, gastrorenal) divert portal blood — and nitrogenous substrates including ammonia — directly to the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic first-pass metabolism. This mechanism can cause recurrent or persistent hyperammonemia and overt HE even when hepatocellular synthetic function is well preserved. The guideline recommends consideration of shunt embolization or reduction in selected patients with intractable shunt-related HE. West Haven criteria grade the clinical severity of HE independent of underlying mechanism.

results.title: Ferenci P et al. Hepatic encephalopathy — definition, nomenclature, diagnosis, and quantification. Hepatology 2002
results.summary: HE classification includes type B (bypass — portosystemic shunting without intrinsic liver disease) and type C (cirrhosis-associated). Large spontaneous portosystemic shunts can produce type B or mixed type B/C encephalopathy. The ammonia level is supportive but not required for diagnosis; clinical presentation and exclusion of alternate causes are central to the West Haven grading.

results.title: Wijdicks EFM. Hepatic Encephalopathy. NEJM 2016
results.summary: Recurrent episodic HE in patients with known portosystemic shunts may mimic transient ischemic attack in elderly patients if liver disease is not overtly apparent. Clinical history of episodic confusion with a known shunt and hyperammonemia should prompt exclusion of HE before vascular attribution.

output.summary: Published guidelines and expert reviews establish that large spontaneous portosystemic shunts — including splenorenal and gastrorenal shunts — cause hyperammonemia and overt HE independent of the degree of hepatocellular synthetic impairment. HE due to shunting (AASLD type B/C) is a recognized entity requiring targeted treatment including lactulose, rifaximin, and specialist evaluation for shunt intervention. Ammonia elevation in the setting of a known large shunt and episodic confusion supports HE; clinical exclusion of alternate neurological causes is standard of care per AASLD/EASL 2014.

output.proposed: Lactulose 30 mL TID + rifaximin 550 mg BID in patient on aspirin 81 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg — HE management review
interactions: Rifaximin: minimal systemic absorption; no clinically significant interaction with aspirin, amlodipine, or atorvastatin at standard dosing
Lactulose: osmotic laxative; no direct pharmacokinetic interactions with current medications; monitor for electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hypernatremia) with prolonged use
Atorvastatin: hepatically metabolized (CYP3A4); mild elevation of transaminases possible in compensated cirrhosis; does not directly raise ammonia or worsen HE at standard doses
Amlodipine: hepatically metabolized; half-life may be prolonged in cirrhosis; at 5 mg, risk of over-exposure is low at Child-Pugh A
contraindications: Benzodiazepines: avoid in known portosystemic shunting and HE — reduced hepatic metabolism and CNS depression worsen encephalopathy
Sedating antihistamines, opioids: avoid — CNS depressants exacerbate HE in the setting of shunting
warnings: Aspirin 81 mg: in cirrhosis, monitor for GI bleeding risk — GI hemorrhage is a common HE precipitant; consider GI prophylaxis if high risk
Lactulose over-titration: target 2-3 soft stools per day — diarrhea causes dehydration, hypokalemia, and paradoxical HE worsening
Rifaximin and atorvastatin: no clinically significant PK interaction at doses used
alternatives: Lactulose 30 mL TID titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day
Rifaximin 550 mg BID — standard secondary prophylaxis per AASLD
Continue aspirin with GI monitoring; no substitution needed unless GI bleed develops

output.consultation_note: Hepatology and interventional radiology consulted regarding large spontaneous splenorenal shunt and recurrent shunt-related HE. Prior CT abdomen (18 months ago) documented a large splenorenal shunt measuring approximately 1.8 cm in diameter with documented portosystemic flow diversion. In the context of recurrent episodic HE, hyperammonemia (118 µmol/L), and well-preserved hepatocellular synthetic function (MELD 7, Child-Pugh A), shunt-related HE is the leading diagnosis. Recommendations: (1) initiate lactulose and rifaximin per AASLD guidelines; (2) cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) with vascular protocol to reassess shunt anatomy and suitability for percutaneous shunt embolization; (3) dietary protein counselling — adequate protein intake maintained but avoid acute high-load boluses; (4) long-term hepatology follow-up for shunt management decision.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy due to large spontaneous splenorenal portosystemic shunt, compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD 7) — West Haven grade II, recurrent episodic; previously mislabeled as TIA (x3) and sundowning from MCI.

differential.diagnosis: Recurrent transient ischemic attack (vertebrobasilar or hemispheric)
differential.key_features: Prior TIA workup (MRI x2 without DWI lesion; normal echo and 30-day monitor) — negative structural/embolic workup does not distinguish TIA from HE; episodic confusion resolving spontaneously fits HE at least as well as TIA; TIA requires imaging evidence or high-risk mechanism.

Episodic prolonged confusion in elderly patient; EEG triphasic-like waveforms raise consideration of NCSE — EEG shows no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures, but NCSE must be actively excluded in recurrent episodic altered mental status.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / sundowning from age-related MCI
differential.key_features: Periventricular white matter changes and age 70 support mild vascular cognitive impairment; however, discrete 6-12 hour episodes with complete recovery do not fit progressive vascular dementia; 'sundowning' diagnosis assigned without considering metabolic cause.

differential.diagnosis: Acute metabolic encephalopathy — other (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia)
differential.key_features: Glucose, sodium, creatinine, and BUN are all normal on comprehensive labs — routine metabolic causes excluded; ammonia is the only markedly abnormal metabolic parameter.

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder / delirium from acute illness
differential.key_features: No fever, no focal infection, no precipitating acute illness identified; asterixis and marked hyperammonemia are not features of primary psychiatric delirium.

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive labs: CMP including AST/ALT/bilirubin/INR/albumin, ammonia, CBC, glucose, electrolytes (Na, K, Mg), BUN/Cr, lactate, blood cultures and urine cultures; serum ethanol. Confirms hepatic function, quantifies ammonia elevation, screens for metabolic precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 118 µmol/L (markedly elevated); near-normal LFTs — bilirubin 1.1, INR 1.1, albumin 3.8; mild AST elevation; platelets low; no metabolic alternative (Na/K/Cr/glucose/lactate near-normal).

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass, or large acute ischemic stroke as the cause of episodic confusion; prerequisite before any LP and necessary given repeated TIA framing.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No hemorrhage, mass, or acute ischemic change; mild age-appropriate atrophy.

optimal_actions.action: MRI brain with DWI — definitive exclusion of acute ischemic TIA/stroke across all territories; given three prior TIA labels and no prior MRI-negative-for-DWI documentation this admission, imaging is required to close the vascular differential.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No acute DWI lesion; no structural explanation for episodic confusion; periventricular white matter changes consistent with mild small-vessel disease only.

optimal_actions.action: Search medical literature — confirm HE due to spontaneous portosystemic shunting in compensated cirrhosis; West Haven grading; AASLD/EASL management framework including shunt-specific considerations.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; shunt-type HE (type B/C), West Haven criteria, lactulose and rifaximin as primary management confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review: review aspirin (GI bleed risk — HE precipitant), atorvastatin (CYP3A4, liver disease), amlodipine (hepatic metabolism), and screen for any added CNS-depressant medications; confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No direct HE-precipitating drugs on current list; GI bleed risk from aspirin noted; no benzodiazepines or opioids present.

optimal_actions.action: Consult hepatology and interventional radiology — coordinate management of shunt-related HE; assess anatomy for shunt embolization candidacy; initiate lactulose and rifaximin; arrange repeat cross-sectional vascular imaging to define shunt.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology and IR input obtained; shunt embolization planning initiated; medical management for HE started.

DaTscan has no role in the HE workup; there is no clinical picture of parkinsonism or nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in the HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy from shunting is the diagnosis and does not require nuclear functional brain imaging.
Carotid duplex was performed in the prior TIA workup and is not part of the HE workup; vascular attribution has been excluded by negative MRI DWI.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect or hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.
In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect on MRI before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Initiate lactulose 30 mL TID (titrate to 2-3 soft stools per day) and rifaximin 550 mg BID.

Recognize that HE due to large spontaneous portosystemic shunt can occur with well-preserved hepatocellular synthetic function (near-normal bilirubin, INR, albumin, MELD 7) — do not dismiss HE because liver tests look near-normal.
Reclassify prior TIA episodes as likely recurrent shunt-related HE; discontinue antiplatelet escalation based on TIA misdiagnosis.
Arrange CT or MRI with vascular protocol of the abdomen to reassess splenorenal shunt anatomy and quantify shunt diameter for embolization candidacy.
Refer for joint hepatology and interventional radiology evaluation for percutaneous shunt embolization or reduction.
Identify dietary precipitant (high protein meal) and constipation as contributors to this episode; provide dietary counselling.
Exclude active GI bleeding (aspirin in cirrhosis — check stool guaiac; GI bleed is a classic HE precipitant).
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute episodic confusion to TIA without first excluding HE in a patient with known portosystemic shunting and hyperammonemia.
Do not dismiss HE diagnosis because hepatocellular synthetic function appears preserved — portosystemic shunting causes HE independent of hepatocellular failure.
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for agitation or anxiety — CNS depressants precipitate and prolong HE in the setting of portosystemic shunting.
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; use acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain management if needed.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect in this patient with altered mental status.

Do not escalate antiplatelet therapy (add clopidogrel, DOAC) based on the prior TIA label without first confirming the vascular diagnosis — anticoagulation in cirrhosis carries bleeding risk and TIA diagnosis is not established.
key_reasoning_points: HE does not require overt hepatic failure: large spontaneous portosystemic shunts (splenorenal, gastrorenal) divert nitrogenous portal blood directly to the systemic circulation, producing hyperammonemia and HE even when hepatocellular synthetic function is well preserved (AASLD/EASL 2014 type B/C HE).

Near-normal bilirubin (1.1), INR (1.1), albumin (3.8), and MELD 7 anchor physicians away from HE — the shunt physiology makes these parameters misleading; the diagnosis rests on hyperammonemia (118 µmol/L), asterixis, episodic clinical presentation, and known large shunt anatomy.

Recurrent episodic confusion lasting 6-12 hours with complete recovery and no DWI lesion on MRI is far more consistent with episodic HE than with TIA — TIA must be established by imaging evidence or a high-risk mechanism, not default diagnosis of exclusion.

Precipitants relevant to shunt-related HE include constipation (2-day history), dietary protein load (large steak dinner), and GI bleeding risk (aspirin in cirrhosis) — identifying and correcting precipitants is as important as initiating lactulose.

EEG showing triphasic-like waveforms and generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges supports a metabolic encephalopathy pattern and excludes NCSE — an important differential in elderly patients with episodic confusion.

Management of refractory shunt-related HE extends beyond lactulose and rifaximin to percutaneous shunt embolization or reduction — hepatology and interventional radiology consultation is essential for long-term management planning.

red_herrings.data_point: Near-normal LFTs: bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, INR 1.1, albumin 3.8 g/dL, AST mildly elevated at 48 U/L — MELD 7
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor away from HE — 'liver looks fine, this cannot be hepatic encephalopathy'; attribute confusion to vascular/neurological cause instead.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Near-normal hepatocellular synthetic function does not exclude HE when a large portosystemic shunt is present; shunt-driven HE occurs independent of hepatocellular failure via direct ammonia bypass of liver first-pass metabolism.

red_herrings.data_point: Three prior episodes labeled TIA by neurology — aspirin prescribed; MCI label for morning confusion episodes
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept the prior TIA diagnosis and pursue further vascular workup (carotid imaging, anticoagulation); dismiss or deprioritize HE because 'neurology already evaluated this.'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior TIA diagnosis does not exclude HE; recurrent episodic 6-12 hour confusion with full recovery, no DWI lesion, no embolic source, and a known large portosystemic shunt is more consistent with recurrent shunt-related HE than TIA; prior workup did not include ammonia level on prior admissions per chart review.

red_herrings.data_point: Periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities (Fazekas 1-2) on MRI — mild left atrial enlargement on fallback echo
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute confusion to cerebrovascular small-vessel disease; pursue vascular neurology workup and cardioembolic evaluation based on LA enlargement.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild white matter changes and LA enlargement are common age-related incidental findings in a 70-year-old; they do not explain acute episodic confusion with full recovery; the absence of DWI lesion and the markedly elevated ammonia (118 µmol/L) reframe the diagnosis.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: HE due to large spontaneous splenorenal shunt in a 70-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis (MELD 7) and near-normal hepatocellular synthetic function — three prior episodes mislabeled as TIA; liver tests appear near-normal anchoring physicians away from HE; diagnosis requires recognizing that portosystemic shunting causes HE independent of hepatocellular failure; ammonia markedly elevated (118 µmol/L) despite preserved bilirubin/INR/albumin.
